concepts.name: Heat
concepts.statement: Heat is the spontaneous transfer of energy due to a temperature difference. When two objects at different temperatures are brought into contact, energy passes from the hotter to the colder one until they reach the same temperature, and no force acts through a distance while it does, so the transfer is not work. Heat is therefore a form of energy in transit: it exists only while the temperature difference drives it, and it ceases once the temperatures are equal.

concepts.name: Heat versus temperature
concepts.statement: We may say the heat was unbearable when we mean the temperature was high. Heat is a form of energy, measured in joules; temperature is not an energy but a measure of the average kinetic energy of the atoms and molecules. The confusion arises because we sense the flow of heat rather than the temperature itself. Keeping the two apart lets the rest of the chapter show that adding heat need not raise a temperature at all.

concepts.name: Units of heat
concepts.statement: Because heat is a form of energy, its SI unit is the joule, but heat is also measured in the calorie, the energy needed to warm 1.00 g of water by 1.00 °C, and most often in the kilocalorie, which warms 1.00 kg of water by the same amount. A food calorie is a kilocalorie, a fact not easily determined from package labeling, and converting among these units is part of almost every problem in the chapter.

concepts.name: Mechanical equivalent of heat
concepts.statement: Doing work can also change the temperature of a substance, and James Prescott Joule's experiments established the mechanical equivalent of heat, the work that produces the same effects as heat transfer. The best modern value is 1.000 kcal = 4186 J, which we treat as the conversion between two units of energy. In Joule's apparatus falling weights turn paddles in water. Gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy, viscosity randomizes it into the motion of the molecules, and the thermometer rises exactly as it would have with heat added instead.

concepts.name: Changing internal energy by heat or work
concepts.statement: Heat added to a system changes its internal energy and usually its temperature, and so does work done on the system, by stirring or by rubbing. A system has a well-defined internal energy, but it does not have a heat content or a work content: once the energy is inside, nothing about the sample says which way it came. This is why the book says heat transfer rather than heat, and it is the idea Chapter 15 will build the first law of thermodynamics on.

concepts.name: Kilocalorie
concepts.statement: The kilocalorie is a unit of heat, 1000 calories, the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1.00 kg of water by 1.00 °C. A food calorie is a kilocalorie.

concepts.name: Factors in heat transfer
concepts.statement: Experiments show that the heat transferred to change a body's temperature depends on three factors: the change in temperature, the mass of the body, and the substance and its phase. Doubling the temperature change of a given mass takes twice the heat, doubling the mass takes twice the heat for the same change, and the same change in the same mass of water takes 10.8 times the heat it takes in copper. The first two follow from the internal energy being proportional to the absolute temperature and to the number of molecules; the third is a property of the material.

concepts.name: Heat and temperature change
concepts.statement: The heat transferred is the mass times the specific heat times the change in temperature, provided there is no phase change and no work is done. The temperature change is the same in kelvin and in degrees Celsius, so either will do, and with heat in kilocalories the specific heat is in kcal/(kg·°C). This is the working equation of the whole chapter, since every later method of heat transfer comes back to the temperature change it produces.

forms.condition: no phase change and no work done

concepts.name: Specific heat
concepts.statement: The specific heat is the amount of heat necessary to change the temperature of 1.00 kg of a substance by 1.00 °C. It depends on the material and its phase, must generally be looked up in a table because there is no simple way to calculate it, and varies little with temperature for most solids and liquids. Water's is among the largest of any material, five times that of glass and ten times that of iron, which is important for sustaining life on Earth.

concepts.name: Finding the temperature rise from work
concepts.statement: When work turns into internal energy, the same equation, solved for the temperature change, gives the rise: the energy delivered divided by the mass and the specific heat of what absorbs it. Truck brakes on a downhill run convert the gravitational potential energy the truck loses into internal energy of the brake material. Because the brakes are small compared with the truck, even a tenth of that energy warms them quickly.

concepts.name: Calorimetry
concepts.statement: When two bodies at different temperatures touch in an insulated container, heat passes from the hotter to the colder until they reach a common temperature. No heat leaves the pair, so the heat the hot body loses is the heat the cold one gains. With signs, the heat into the cold body is positive, the heat out of the hot body is negative, and the two sum to zero. This is a calorimetry problem, and calorimetry measures the heat content of foods and the specific heats of materials.

forms.condition: no heat exchanged with the surroundings

concepts.name: Finding the final temperature of two bodies
concepts.statement: Solving the calorimetry balance for the final temperature gives a weighted average of the two starting temperatures, each weighted by its body's mass times specific heat. The pan at 150 °C and the water at 20.0 °C meet at 59.1 °C, much closer to the water, because water's specific heat is more than four times aluminum's and its mass times specific heat is the larger weight. The skill is to write the heat lost and the heat gained in terms of the one unknown temperature and then collect the terms.

forms.condition: two bodies exchanging heat with no phase change

concepts.name: Water moderating temperature
concepts.statement: Because water has a greater specific heat than most common substances, it undergoes a small temperature change for a given heat transfer. A large body of water such as a lake needs a great deal of heat to warm appreciably, so its temperature stays nearly constant through a day even when the air's changes a great deal, while it does change over the longer times from summer to winter. Land warms and cools faster than water, which is what drives land breezes and sea breezes.

concepts.name: Latent heat
concepts.statement: Heat transfer causes no temperature change while a substance changes phase. The energy goes into breaking the cohesive bonds between molecules rather than into their kinetic energy, so ice at 0 °C stays at 0 °C until all of it has melted. The same energy comes back out, usually as thermal energy, when the bonds form again in freezing or condensation. The heat that changes the phase of a mass is that mass times a latent heat coefficient, a material constant. It is latent, or hidden, because the energy enters or leaves without changing the temperature.

concepts.name: Heat of fusion
concepts.statement: The latent heat of fusion is the heat that melts a kilogram of a substance at its melting point, and the kilogram releases the same heat when it freezes. For water it is 334 kJ/kg, enough to warm a kilogram of liquid water from 0 °C to 79.8 °C. A bag of ice at 0 °C therefore absorbs far more energy than a bag of water at the same temperature, and water freezing on a sprayed orchard warms the trees.

concepts.name: Heat of vaporization
concepts.statement: The latent heat of vaporization is the heat that turns a kilogram of liquid into vapor at the boiling point, and the vapor releases the same heat when it condenses. For water it is 2256 kJ/kg, nearly seven times its heat of fusion, so boiling away a kilogram of water costs more than raising it from ice-cold to boiling. Condensation on a glass of iced tea releases energy into the glass and speeds the melting of the ice.

concepts.name: Heating curve of water
concepts.statement: Adding heat to ice at −20 °C traces a graph with slopes and plateaus. The temperature rises linearly while the ice warms, stops at 0 °C while the ice melts and every joule goes into the phase change, rises again more slowly through the liquid because water's specific heat is twice ice's, stops at 100 °C for a much longer plateau while the water boils, and rises once more as steam. The plateaus are the latent heats, and their lengths beside the slopes show that the energy of a phase change is enormous compared with that of a temperature change.

concepts.name: Evaporation below the boiling point
concepts.statement: Water evaporates at temperatures below its boiling point, and it costs more energy per kilogram to do so, because the molecules have less kinetic energy to draw on: at body temperature the heat of vaporization is 2430 kJ/kg, about ten percent higher than at 100 °C. Perspiration takes this heat from the skin, which is why sweating cools, and high humidity slows evaporation so that the sweat stays on your brow. The same evaporation is why air temperatures in humid climates rarely rise above 35 °C.

concepts.name: Condensation and freezing release heat
concepts.statement: To make vapor condense or liquid freeze, you must remove exactly the energy the phase change absorbed in the other direction, and the surroundings receive it. That is why condensation on a cold glass speeds the melting of the ice inside, why temperatures in humid weather rarely fall below the dew point, why spraying an orchard with water protects it from a hard frost, and why freezing water stays at 0 °C and no colder.

concepts.name: Heat of sublimation
concepts.statement: Sublimation is the transition from the solid phase directly to the vapor phase, as when snow disappears without a trace of liquid, dry ice makes its smoke, or frost forms on a cold window from vapor alone. It occurs because the equilibrium vapor pressure of a solid is not zero. The energy required is the mass times the heat of sublimation, a constant of the same order as the other latent heats, so dry ice is an effective coolant and frosting releases energy.

forms.condition: solid to vapor, or vapor to solid

concepts.name: Finding the final temperature with a phase change
concepts.statement: When a phase change takes part in a heat exchange, work the problem in stages. The heat that melts the ice, then the heat that warms the melted water, balance the heat the other body gives up, with every term in the one unknown final temperature. Try the problem without a phase change first. If the temperature change would carry a body past a melting or boiling point, go back and do it in steps, and check at the end that you have missed no phase change.

forms.condition: the soda and the ice exchange heat with nothing else

concepts.name: Three methods of heat transfer
concepts.statement: Whenever there is a temperature difference, heat transfer occurs, and every process by which it does takes place by only three methods: conduction, convection and radiation. All three have one thing in common, that they transfer heat solely because of a temperature difference, and we control their rates by choosing materials, controlling the movement of air and choosing colors. A fireplace shows all three at once.

concepts.name: Conduction
concepts.statement: Conduction is heat transfer through stationary matter by physical contact. The matter is stationary on the large scale, though its atoms and molecules are in thermal motion at any temperature above absolute zero, and the heat passes between the electric burner of a stove and the bottom of a pan, or from a hot floor into the sole of a foot, without anything moving from one place to the other.

concepts.name: Convection
concepts.statement: Convection is heat transfer by the macroscopic movement of a fluid. The fluid itself carries the energy from one place to another, as the air does in a forced-air furnace, in the draft up a chimney and in the weather, and as water does in the cooling system of a car.

concepts.name: Radiation
concepts.statement: Heat transfer by radiation occurs when microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light or another form of electromagnetic radiation is emitted or absorbed. The Sun warms the Earth this way across empty space, a fire warms the room mostly this way, and the human body radiates infrared whether or not anything touches it.

concepts.name: Conduction by molecular collisions
concepts.statement: The molecules of a hotter body have the greater average kinetic energy, and when a fast molecule and a slow one collide at the surface where two bodies touch, energy passes from the faster to the slower. The cumulative effect of all the collisions is a net flux of heat from the hot body to the cold one that grows with the temperature difference and with the area of contact, and that falls to zero when the temperatures are equal. Because it relies on random motion, conduction is slow over distances larger than a molecule's reach.

concepts.name: Rate of conductive heat transfer
concepts.statement: The rate at which heat flows through a slab of material by conduction is proportional to the temperature difference across it and to its area, inversely proportional to its thickness, and set by a constant of the material, its thermal conductivity. Experiment revealed and confirms these four factors, and the equation holds whether the slab is window glass or walrus blubber. It gives the rate in watts.

concepts.name: Thermal conductivity
concepts.statement: Thermal conductivity measures a material's ability to conduct heat, and it spans more than four orders of magnitude across common substances. The best thermal conductors, silver, copper, gold and aluminum, are also the best electrical conductors, because of the density of free electrons in them, and cooks use utensils made of them. Styrofoam, fiberglass, wool and down conduct poorly because they trap many small pockets of air, whose own conductivity is among the lowest of all.

concepts.name: R factor
concepts.statement: A good insulator combines a small conductivity with a large thickness, and the ratio of thickness to conductivity is the R factor. The rate of conductive heat transfer is inversely proportional to it, so the larger the R factor, the better the insulation. Household insulation quotes it, still in non-metric units: 3.5-inch fiberglass batts rate 11 and 6.5-inch batts 19.

concepts.name: Finding the mass melted by conduction
concepts.statement: The conduction equation gives a rate; multiplying it by a time gives the heat, and that heat may be spent on a phase change. A Styrofoam ice box in a hot car trunk lets heat in at a rate set by its walls, and over a day that heat melts a mass of ice equal to the total heat divided by the heat of fusion. The skill is to carry a rate into an amount and an amount into a mass, keeping each step's units.

concepts.name: Finding the temperature difference from a heat flow
concepts.statement: Solved the other way, the conduction equation gives the temperature difference that a known rate of heat transfer keeps across a slab. Through the aluminum bottom of a pan boiling away a gram of water a second, 2.26 kW crosses with a difference of only 5.33 °C, because aluminum conducts so well; across a ceramic stove top of the same area the same rate would need a thousand degrees. A small temperature difference with a large heat flow is the mark of a good conductor.

concepts.name: Scaling of the conduction rate
concepts.statement: Because area is the product of two lengths and thickness is one, doubling every dimension of a slab quadruples the area and only doubles the thickness, and the rate of conductive heat transfer doubles. Comparisons of this kind, a thin window against a thick wall, a callus against a bare sole, are answered by ratios of the four factors without evaluating either rate.

concepts.name: Natural convection
concepts.statement: Buoyant forces drive natural convection. A heated fluid expands, its density falls, and it rises through the cooler, denser fluid around it, which sinks to take its place; the loop that forms carries heat with the moving matter. A gravity furnace heats a house this way, a pot of water on a stove circulates this way, and ocean currents and the atmosphere carry energy across the globe this way. Forced convection, in a car's cooling system or the blood vessels of the skin, is the same transport driven by a pump.

concepts.name: Finding heat transfer by convection
concepts.statement: To find the heat convection carries, find the mass of fluid moved, from its density and volume, and multiply by its specific heat and its temperature change. Divide by the time in which that mass is replaced to get the rate. Warming the air of a house by 10.0 °C, when all of it is replaced every half hour, takes 4.64 kW, the power of forty-six 100 W bulbs, which is why houses are weather-stripped.

forms.condition: the mass m of fluid is moved or replaced in the time t

concepts.name: Wind chill
concepts.statement: A cold wind is much more chilling than still cold air, because convection combines with conduction in the body to increase the rate at which energy leaves it. Wind-chill factors are the temperatures of still air that would produce the same rate of cooling as air of a given temperature and speed, and they are a dramatic reminder of convection's ability to transfer heat faster than conduction: a 15.0 m/s wind at 0 °C chills like still air at about −18 °C.

concepts.name: Trapped air is an insulator
concepts.statement: Air transfers heat rapidly by convection but conducts poorly, so whether it insulates depends on whether it can flow. The 9 cm space inside a house wall is large enough for convection, so builders fill it with insulation to stop the air moving. The 1 cm gap of a double-paned window is too small for convection and takes advantage of air's low conductivity. Fur, feathers and fiberglass all trap air in pockets too small for convection, which is why they are light and warm.

concepts.name: Evaporation rate
concepts.statement: When convection is accompanied by a phase change, the moving fluid carries the latent heat with it, and the rate at which mass evaporates to remove a given power is that power divided by the heat of vaporization. Sweat evaporating from the skin can carry away a resting body's 120 W at about 3 g per minute, even when the air is as warm as the skin, provided air flow replaces the saturated air. The same process carries heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, drives thunderheads 20 km into the stratosphere by positive feedback, and lets a melting iceberg cool the sea it drifts through.

forms.condition: the heat is carried away by evaporation alone

concepts.name: Radiation spectrum and temperature
concepts.statement: A hot body emits electromagnetic waves that need no medium to travel, and shorter wavelengths carry more energy. Because a body radiates more heat at higher temperatures, its color changes with its temperature: from the infrared you feel from a stove element that has not yet begun to glow, to red, to the yellow and white of steel in a blast furnace. The spectrum of an ideal radiator rises dramatically with temperature, and its peak shifts toward the visible and the ultraviolet.

concepts.name: Absorbers and emitters
concepts.statement: The rate of heat transfer by radiation is largely determined by the color of the object. Black absorbs best and radiates best, so black asphalt is hotter than gray sidewalk by day and colder by night; white and silver absorb poorly and radiate poorly, reflecting radiation like a mirror. An ideal radiator is the same color as an ideal absorber, and the balance of radiation into and out of an object depends only on how well the object itself emits and absorbs.

concepts.name: Emissivity
concepts.statement: The emissivity is a measure of how well an object radiates. An ideal jet-black radiator, a black body, has an emissivity of 1, a perfect reflector has 0, and real objects fall between: tungsten filaments about 0.5, carbon black about 0.99, and skin 0.97 in the infrared, so that we are all nearly black in the infrared whatever our visible color. The Earth's average emissivity is about 0.65, complicated by its varying cloud cover.

concepts.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
concepts.statement: The rate of heat transfer by emitted radiation is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant times the emissivity times the surface area times the fourth power of the absolute temperature in kelvin. The radiation rate goes as the surface area, which is why knocking apart the coals of a fire makes it noticeably hotter to stand near, and it goes as the fourth power of the temperature, a remarkably strong dependence that the next two results turn on. The temperature must be absolute; a Celsius value in this equation is wrong.

concepts.name: Fourth-power dependence of radiation
concepts.statement: Because the radiated power goes as the fourth power of the absolute temperature, small temperature differences produce detectable differences in radiation: a body at 40 °C radiates about 30 percent more than the same body at 20 °C, and skin at 34.0 °C radiates 1.31 percent more than at 33.0 °C, enough for a thermograph to map. At larger ratios the effect is enormous, a radiator at four times the absolute temperature emitting 256 times the power.

concepts.name: Net rate of heat transfer by radiation
terms: net rate of heat transfer by radiation
concepts.statement: All objects emit and absorb radiation, so the net rate is the absorption minus the emission, which for an object at one temperature surrounded by an environment at another is the Stefan-Boltzmann expression in the difference of the two fourth powers, with the emissivity of the object alone. It does not matter whether the surroundings are white, gray or black; when the surroundings are hotter the net transfer is into the object, and when they are colder it is out. An unclothed person in a 22.0 °C room loses about 99 W this way.

forms.condition: an object at T_1 in surroundings of uniform temperature T_2, both in kelvin

concepts.name: Greenhouse effect
concepts.statement: The Earth receives almost all its energy as radiation from the Sun and radiates energy back into a dark sky at about 3 K, and its steady temperature is the balance of the two. The atmosphere is transparent to the Sun's visible light and most of its infrared, but the infrared the cooler Earth emits is at longer wavelengths that carbon dioxide and water vapor absorb and re-radiate, part of it back to the surface, which keeps the Earth about 40 °C warmer than it would be with no atmosphere. Eunice Newton Foote first measured this in flasks of carbon dioxide left in the sun, and the effect is central to global warming from the gases that industry and farming emit.

concepts.name: Solving heat transfer problems
concepts.statement: To solve a problem in heat transfer, identify which of the three methods is at work and reach for the right relation. Conduction uses the conduction equation with a conductivity from the table; convection uses the temperature-change or latent-heat equation for the mass it carries; radiation uses the net radiation equation for exchange with the surroundings. List the knowns and unknowns, solve the equation for the unknown before putting in numbers, and check the answer for sense: a person cannot warm by 36 °C in a day, and a window cannot lose 1.46 kW.

concepts.name: Stefan-Boltzmann constant
concepts.statement: The Stefan-Boltzmann constant sets the rate at which a surface radiates for a given area, emissivity and absolute temperature. Its value is 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ J/(s·m²·K⁴).
